title: Registration and device-enrollment data can reveal the homeowner's identity
description: The flow carries account-registration details and device-enrollment metadata from the homeowner to the Home Hub. Names, email/phone, account identifiers, home address, and device identifiers/serial numbers can directly identify or strongly single out the homeowner or household when received and processed by the Home Hub.
assumptions: Assumes registration includes personal account details and enrollment includes device identifiers tied to a household.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context only gives applicable threat types, not detailed node ids.

title: Enrollment metadata may enable linking of devices and account to the same household
description: Combining account-registration data with camera/sensor enrollment data allows the Home Hub to link multiple devices, credentials, and household attributes to one homeowner profile. This can create a consolidated view of the household and its installed monitoring equipment.
assumptions: Assumes the Home Hub stores or correlates account and device-enrollment records under a common account or household identifier.
uncertainty_note: Detailed threat-tree node id is approximate; applicability of linkability is high for combined registration and enrollment flows.

title: Enrollment reveals presence and characteristics of in-home surveillance devices
description: The flow discloses privacy-sensitive facts about the household, such as the existence, number, type, and placement-related characteristics of cameras and sensors being enrolled. This can reveal aspects of the home's layout, security posture, occupancy concerns, or lifestyle.
assumptions: Assumes enrollment includes device type, model, room/location label, or similar setup metadata.
uncertainty_note: Specific disclosed attributes depend on the enrollment protocol; room/location details may or may not be present.

title: Homeowner may be unable to prove or contest registration and enrollment actions
description: If the Home Hub does not provide verifiable records, the homeowner may later be unable to demonstrate what account details were submitted, which devices were enrolled, or whether consent and setup actions actually occurred. This creates privacy-relevant repudiation risk around onboarding actions.
assumptions: Assumes lack of trustworthy audit trail, receipts, or user-visible confirmation for registration and enrollment events.
uncertainty_note: Repudiation is included because onboarding actions often need proof, but actual risk depends on whether the system already provides confirmations/logs.

title: The homeowner may be unaware of the full extent of personal and device data collected during onboarding
description: During account registration and device enrollment, the Home Hub may collect more data than the homeowner expects, such as persistent device identifiers, network information, location labels, or telemetry needed for setup. If this collection is not made transparent, the homeowner cannot adequately understand the privacy impact.
assumptions: Assumes onboarding UX does not clearly explain all collected fields and their purposes.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate; threat applicability depends on the transparency of the registration/enrollment interface.

title: Registration and enrollment may occur without sufficiently informed or granular consent
description: The onboarding flow may bundle account creation, device enrollment, telemetry collection, and future data processing under broad terms, preventing the homeowner from giving specific, informed, and freely given consent for each privacy-relevant purpose.
assumptions: Assumes the system relies on consent or similar user agreement for some onboarding-related processing and does not offer granular choices.
uncertainty_note: Consent/compliance obligations depend on jurisdiction and legal basis; included because onboarding commonly raises consent and notice issues.

title: Registration and enrollment data may be used beyond the homeowner's expectations
description: Personal details and device-enrollment information provided for setup may later be used for secondary purposes such as analytics, profiling, product improvement, or sharing with third parties, exceeding the original onboarding purpose understood by the homeowner.
assumptions: Assumes purpose limitation is not strictly enforced and secondary uses are technically or organizationally possible.
uncertainty_note: Threat depends on downstream governance and stated purposes, which are not specified in the flow description.

title: Temporary access code can identify or single out a guest
description: The temporary access code entered by the guest may function as a unique token tied to a specific guest invitation, booking, or visit window. When the Home Hub receives it, the code can enable identification of the guest or at least distinguish this guest session from others.
assumptions: Applies if temporary codes are unique per guest, stay, or time window and are logged or otherwise associated with a person or household event.
uncertainty_note: Threat-tree node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context did not include the specific Identifiability subtree.

title: Guest access-code entry may be detectable by observing the interaction
description: Entering a temporary access code at the Home Hub reveals that someone is attempting to access the home at a particular time. Even if the code value is protected, the act of submission and resulting unlock attempt may disclose the guest's presence or visit pattern.
assumptions: Applies if the Home Hub, nearby observers, or connected components can observe code-entry events, timestamps, or unlock attempts.
uncertainty_note: Threat-tree node id is approximate; the retrieved context did not provide the Detectability subtree for this specific case.

title: Guest may be unaware that entering the temporary code shares personal data
description: The guest may not realize that submitting the temporary access code to the Home Hub can disclose personal data such as presence at the property, time of arrival, and a guest-specific identifier embedded in or linked to the code.
assumptions: Applies if the interface does not clearly explain what data is collected, inferred, or logged when the code is entered.

title: Temporary access-code processing may exceed consent or expected purpose
description: The guest may provide the temporary code solely to unlock the front door, while the Home Hub may also log, retain, correlate, or reuse the code-entry event for analytics, monitoring, or profiling beyond what the guest reasonably expects or has consented to.
assumptions: Applies if code-entry data or associated metadata are processed for secondary purposes or without an appropriate legal basis, notice, or consent mechanism.
uncertainty_note: Threat-tree node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context did not include the Non-compliance subtree.

title: Event log enables linkage of household activity over time
description: Writing motion, door, and other sensor events into a single local event log creates a consolidated history that can be linked across timestamps, sensors, and rooms. This may allow reconstruction of routines, occupancy patterns, and correlations between events that identify or single out residents.
assumptions: Sensor events are associated with a household, device identifiers, room/location labels, or precise timestamps sufficient to correlate records over time.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context gives applicable threat types for Process→DataStore but not detailed LINDDUN Pro node ids for linkability.

title: Local event log may enable inference of sensitive household behavior
description: Even if raw entries only contain motion/door/sensor events, the accumulated log can reveal inferred information such as sleep schedules, presence/absence, religious or health-related routines, and periods when the home is unoccupied. These inferences arise from patterns in stored events rather than explicit fields alone.
assumptions: The log retains sufficiently granular timestamps and event types to support behavioral inference.
uncertainty_note: Detailed threat-tree node id is approximate; inference clearly applies, but exact node numbering was not provided in the retrieved context.

title: Residents may be unable to deny logged events attributed to them or their household
description: Persisting sensor events in a local log can create records later used as evidence that a person was present, absent, or active at a certain time. If events are treated as authoritative without mechanisms to contest accuracy, affected individuals may be unable to repudiate conclusions drawn from the log.
assumptions: The system or operators may rely on the log for audits, alerts, or retrospective investigation of household activity.
uncertainty_note: Repudiation risk depends on whether the log is used as evidence about individuals rather than only for transient device operation.

title: Stored event history can make household members detectable
description: The act of recording sensor events to the local event log makes the presence and activities of household members detectable within the system. Anyone with access to the datastore can determine whether someone is home, moving, entering, or leaving based on logged events and timestamps.
assumptions: The datastore is accessible to some local administrator, service process, or attacker beyond the immediate sensing function.
uncertainty_note: Exact detectability node id is approximate; applicability is strong because the flow explicitly stores presence/activity events.

title: Excessive retention of raw sensor events in the local log discloses more personal data than necessary
description: Writing all motion, door, and sensor events to persistent local storage may constitute avoidable disclosure if the full raw event history is not strictly necessary for the hub's purpose. The log can expose intimate occupancy and behavior data to any party or component that can access the datastore, contrary to data minimization.
assumptions: Not all raw events need to be stored persistently, or they are retained longer or at finer granularity than required for functionality.
uncertainty_note: Dd.1.1 is selected by best judgement from general data-disclosure/minimization concepts; retrieved context supports Dd applicability but not this exact node id.

title: Residents may be unaware that detailed in-home activity is being logged
description: If the Home Hub silently writes motion, door, and sensor events to a local event log, residents and visitors may not understand that their in-home activities are persistently recorded, what categories are stored, or how long the data remains available.
assumptions: The system lacks clear notice, indicators, or accessible explanations about local logging behavior and retention.
uncertainty_note: Unawareness is plausible for this flow, but depends on the product's transparency and user interface.

title: Persistent logging of household sensor events may exceed consent or user expectations
description: Recording detailed motion, door, and sensor events in a local datastore may go beyond the consent given by residents if they expected real-time automation only, not persistent storage of behavioral history. This creates a risk that collection and retention are not aligned with the purposes communicated to data subjects.
assumptions: Consent or user expectations are limited to immediate device control/automation and do not explicitly cover persistent event-history storage.
uncertainty_note: Non-compliance depends on the actual legal basis, notices, and consent design; exact node id is approximate.

title: Upload flow reveals sensitive video content to an unintended observer
description: Recorded camera clips uploaded from the Home Hub to cloud storage may contain highly sensitive personal data about residents, visitors, routines, interiors, and activities. If the upload channel or endpoint handling is insufficiently protected, the disclosure can expose intimate household information beyond the intended storage purpose.
assumptions: Assumes the flow carries identifiable household video clips and that confidentiality of the transfer and receiving endpoint is relevant to privacy.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best judgement from LINDDUN disclosure threat structure; exact subnode may vary by threat-tree version.

title: Uploaded clips can be linked to a specific household or resident
description: The upload of recorded camera clips to cloud storage can enable identification of data subjects through faces, voices, home interiors, timestamps, device identifiers, account identifiers, or network metadata. Even if clips are not explicitly labeled with names, the flow may still permit direct or indirect identification.
assumptions: Assumes clips or associated metadata contain direct or indirect identifiers.
uncertainty_note: Exact identification subnode id is inferred from general LINDDUN identification threats rather than retrieved context.

title: Repeated clip uploads enable linkage of events and behavior over time
description: Successive uploads of camera clips to the same cloud storage context can be correlated using account identifiers, device identifiers, timestamps, location context, or recurring visual patterns. This may allow linking separate recordings into detailed profiles of household behavior, occupancy, and routines.
assumptions: Assumes the cloud service can associate multiple uploads with the same account, device, or household.
uncertainty_note: Exact linkage subnode id is inferred from standard LINDDUN linkage threats.

title: Cloud-stored video enables broad detectability of residents' presence and activities
description: Once uploaded, stored camera clips make the presence, absence, movements, and activities of residents or visitors detectable to parties with access to the cloud storage or its metadata. Even metadata such as upload times and clip frequency can reveal occupancy patterns.
assumptions: Assumes stored clips or metadata are accessible to cloud operators, administrators, attackers, or other unauthorized parties.
uncertainty_note: Specific detectability subnode is selected by best judgement; exact numbering may differ across LINDDUN Pro versions.

title: Stored camera clips may be retained longer than necessary
description: Cloud video storage may keep uploaded camera clips beyond the period necessary for the stated surveillance or security purpose. Excessive retention increases privacy risk by preserving detailed records of household life longer than justified.
assumptions: Assumes retention limits are absent, unclear, or not enforced for uploaded clips.

title: Residents or visitors may be unaware that clips are uploaded to cloud storage
description: People captured by the home camera system may not understand that recordings are not only stored locally but also uploaded to a remote cloud service. This lack of awareness can undermine informed expectations about where footage goes, who may access it, and how long it is kept.
assumptions: Assumes the system does not clearly communicate cloud upload behavior to affected individuals.
uncertainty_note: Exact unawareness subnode id is inferred from general LINDDUN unawareness threats.

title: Insufficient evidence of consent or authorization for cloud upload of recordings
description: The system may upload recorded clips to cloud storage without maintaining adequate evidence that the homeowner configured this behavior knowingly, or that other affected individuals were appropriately informed where required. This can make it difficult to demonstrate that the upload was authorized or properly agreed to.
assumptions: Assumes consent, configuration choice, or other authorization for cloud upload should be demonstrable in this context.
uncertainty_note: Applicability depends on legal basis and product design; exact repudiation subnode id is inferred.

title: Excessive disclosure in real-time motion alert payload
description: The Home Hub may forward more personal data than necessary to the mobile app backend in a real-time motion alert, such as precise timestamps, device identifiers, household identifiers, location/context metadata, or raw sensor details when only a minimal alert event is needed. This would constitute avoidable disclosure of personal data across the process boundary.
assumptions: Assumes the alert contains personal or household-related metadata beyond the minimum needed for backend notification handling.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is best-judgement based on LINDDUN Pro Data Disclosure/minimality concepts; retrieved context supports Dd generally but does not provide the exact subtree id.

title: Linkability of motion events via persistent hub or household identifiers
description: If each motion alert includes stable identifiers for the hub, account, household, or sensor, the backend can link multiple alerts over time to the same home and infer occupancy patterns, routines, and behavior. The privacy threat is the ability to correlate separate events that need not be linkable for the alerting purpose.
assumptions: Assumes persistent identifiers are transmitted with each alert and that backend processing does not sufficiently separate or rotate them.
uncertainty_note: Exact LINDDUN Pro subtree id is inferred from standard linkability patterns; context confirms L is applicable to Process->Process flows but not the precise node.

title: Identifiability of residents from motion alert content
description: Motion alerts may directly or indirectly identify a resident or household when combined with account identifiers, address-linked hub IDs, or fine-grained timing/context. Even if the alert is about motion rather than a named person, the data may still make individuals identifiable to the backend.
assumptions: Assumes the backend can associate the hub or account with a natural person or household members.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree id is best judgement; applicability of identifiability is strong if backend account mapping exists.

title: Backend can infer presence and daily routines from received motion alerts
description: By receiving real-time motion alerts over time, the mobile app backend can derive sensitive information such as when occupants are home, asleep, away, or following recurring routines. This creates a detectability/privacy-observability risk because the backend can observe and distinguish private household activity states from the flow.
assumptions: Assumes alerts are retained or processed over time rather than handled ephemerally.
uncertainty_note: Detectability subtree id is inferred; context only establishes that D is applicable for this interaction type.

title: Motion alert transmission may exceed user consent or expected purpose
description: Forwarding motion alerts from the Home Hub to the backend may be non-compliant if users were not adequately informed that occupancy-related events would be sent to a backend service, or if the alerts are used for purposes beyond immediate notification delivery. This creates a privacy non-compliance risk tied to transparency, purpose limitation, and lawful basis.
assumptions: Assumes consent, notice, or contractual necessity for backend transmission is absent, unclear, or broader than users reasonably expect.
uncertainty_note: This depends strongly on the actual notice/consent and purpose specification; included because occupancy data is sensitive in context.

title: Excessive content in motion notification discloses personal data
description: The backend may include more personal data than necessary in the push notification payload or visible notification text, such as camera snapshot previews, exact timestamps, device/location labels, or occupancy-related details. Because notifications are delivered across platform and network boundaries and may be exposed on the phone lock screen, this creates avoidable disclosure of the homeowner's personal data beyond what is needed to alert them.
assumptions: The notification contains or could contain personal data beyond a minimal alert, and the phone may display notification content outside the app context (e.g., lock screen or wearable mirroring).
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best judgement for explicit/excessive disclosure on a data flow; retrieved context confirms Dd applies to Process->ExternalEntity flows but does not provide the exact subtree id.

title: Notification metadata can reveal household activity patterns
description: Even if the notification text is minimal, the fact, timing, frequency, and source of motion-detected notifications can allow inference of sensitive information such as when residents are home, asleep, away, or moving in specific areas. This flow therefore risks inference of private behavior from metadata and event patterns.
assumptions: An observer with access to the device notifications, notification logs, or correlated backend/platform metadata can observe timing and recurrence of alerts.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree id is approximate; the applicability of inference is strong, but the precise LINDDUN Pro node numbering may vary by threat-tree version.

title: Persistent notification identifiers may enable linkability of homeowner events
description: If push tokens, stable device identifiers, account identifiers, or recurring event identifiers are embedded in or consistently associated with this notification flow, separate motion events can be linked to the same homeowner or household over time. This enables correlation of activity across sessions, devices, or services.
assumptions: The push delivery ecosystem or payload handling uses stable identifiers or correlatable metadata across multiple notifications.
uncertainty_note: Linkability depends on implementation details of push payloads and identifiers; included because such identifiers are common in mobile notification architectures.

title: Notification content may identify the homeowner or household
description: The notification may directly identify the homeowner or their household by including names, address labels, camera names, or other uniquely identifying descriptors. Even without explicit names, a uniquely named home or device can make the data subject identifiable to anyone who sees the notification.
assumptions: Notification text or metadata contains direct or quasi-identifiers such as user name, home name, room name, or device label.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree id is approximate; identifiability clearly applies if notification content includes direct or quasi-identifiers.

title: Homeowner may be unaware of notification disclosure contexts
description: The homeowner may not realize that motion notifications can appear on lock screens, wearables, shared devices, notification histories, or be processed by mobile platform push providers. This reduces user awareness of how and where personal event data is exposed through the notification flow.
assumptions: The system does not clearly explain notification visibility, third-party push delivery, or device-level exposure settings.
uncertainty_note: Usawareness is plausible for this flow, but exact applicability depends on what notice and controls the app provides.

title: Motion notifications may be sent without sufficiently specific consent or user control
description: If the backend sends motion-detected notifications by default, or with insufficient granularity over which sensors/events generate alerts and what content is shown, the disclosure of personal event data may exceed the homeowner's consent or expectations. This creates a non-compliance risk with consent, data minimization, and privacy-by-default obligations.
assumptions: Notification preferences are enabled by default or lack granular controls over event types, content richness, and lock-screen visibility.
uncertainty_note: Non-compliance depends on jurisdiction and actual consent/control design; included because privacy-by-default and minimization are commonly relevant to push notifications.

title: Shared analytics may remain linkable to individual users or devices
description: Although described as aggregated device-usage analytics, the backend may still transmit stable device, account, cohort, timestamp, or event attributes that allow the vendor to link multiple reports to the same user, device, household, or small group over time, especially when combined with the vendor's existing datasets.
assumptions: Assumes the aggregation is not fully anonymizing and that some persistent or quasi-identifying attributes are included in the payload or metadata.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context gives applicable threat types/positions but not detailed node ids.

title: Vendor may infer identities from aggregated analytics
description: The cloud analytics vendor may be able to identify a user, device, or small population segment from the received analytics by combining aggregates with auxiliary information such as IP ranges, customer account context, app version rollout timing, geography, or other datasets already held by the vendor.
assumptions: Assumes the vendor has access to auxiliary data and that some aggregates are sufficiently granular to support singling out or re-identification.
uncertainty_note: Applies if aggregation granularity is fine enough to permit re-identification; exact threat-tree node id is approximate.

title: Analytics disclosure to the vendor exceeds user expectations
description: Sharing device-usage analytics with an external analytics vendor discloses personal or behavioral information to a third party. Even if aggregated, the data may reveal app usage patterns, feature adoption, locale, device characteristics, or sensitive behavioral trends that users did not expect to be shared outside the primary service provider.
assumptions: Assumes the analytics contain information about user or device behavior that is not strictly necessary for core service delivery.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate; disclosure risk is clear but depends on the actual fields shared and aggregation level.

title: Secondary analytics use by the vendor may be unclear or overly broad
description: Once the analytics reach the cloud analytics vendor, the data may be used for purposes beyond the mobile service's stated purpose, such as product improvement across customers, benchmarking, model training, profiling, or retention for the vendor's own business operations, reducing users' awareness and control over how their data is used.
assumptions: Assumes contractual or technical controls do not strictly limit the vendor to a narrow processor role.
uncertainty_note: This is a common Process→ExternalEntity privacy risk, but applicability depends on the vendor contract and configured service settings; node id is approximate.

title: Third-party analytics sharing may lack a valid legal basis or exceed consent
description: Transferring device-usage analytics to an external analytics vendor may be non-compliant if the sharing is not covered by a valid legal basis, if required consent for analytics/third-party sharing was not obtained, if opt-out signals are ignored, or if data-processing, cross-border transfer, or retention obligations are not properly addressed.
assumptions: Assumes the analytics relate to personal data or can reasonably be linked to individuals/devices under applicable law.
uncertainty_note: Compliance depends heavily on jurisdiction, consent design, and contractual safeguards; exact node id is approximate.

title: Backend can link retrieved video clips to a specific homeowner account
description: When P2 retrieves a stored video clip from DS2 for playback, the request and returned clip metadata/content can be associated with the authenticated homeowner account, device, household, and time of access. This enables linkage between viewing events and an identifiable individual or household beyond the bare need to fetch the clip.
assumptions: Assumes the backend logs or otherwise retains identifiers such as account ID, device ID, household ID, clip ID, or timestamps for retrieval operations.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best judgment because the retrieved context did not include a linkage subtree excerpt.

title: Backend can identify the homeowner from video retrieval requests
description: The retrieval flow to P2 likely contains account/session identifiers and clip references that allow P2 to identify which homeowner is requesting playback. If identification is not necessary for all downstream handling, this creates an identifiability threat at the receiving process.
assumptions: Assumes playback requests are authenticated and tied to a user account or household.
uncertainty_note: Specific tree node id is approximate; retrieved context did not provide the identifiability subtree.

title: Video content and access patterns may be detectable by backend operators or observers
description: By retrieving the stored clip into P2, the backend can observe that a particular clip exists and is being played back at a particular time. Even if only authorized internally, this makes the homeowner's surveillance footage and viewing behavior detectable within the backend environment.
assumptions: Assumes P2 or its operational telemetry exposes clip identifiers, timestamps, or content/metadata to administrators, logs, or monitoring systems.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is approximate because the retrieved context did not include detectability subtree details.

title: Retrieval metadata may disclose sensitive household behavior
description: The clip itself and its retrieval metadata can disclose private information such as occupancy patterns, visitor presence, routines, or incidents at the homeowner's property. Bringing the clip into P2 for playback increases the chance that such information is exposed through processing, caching, logging, or internal access.
assumptions: Assumes the stored video contains personal or household activity and that P2 may temporarily store, transform, or log clip data or metadata.
uncertainty_note: Specific disclosure subtree node is selected by best judgment; no exact subtree citation was retrieved.

title: Homeowner may be unaware of backend-side handling during playback retrieval
description: When the backend retrieves a clip for playback, the homeowner may not be aware of additional backend-side processing such as caching, logging, analytics, or internal retention of access events. This can undermine transparency about how playback data is handled.
assumptions: Assumes the service does not clearly communicate all backend processing associated with playback retrieval.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is approximate because the retrieved context did not include the unawareness subtree.

title: Playback retrieval data may be retained longer than necessary
description: P2 may store retrieved clips temporarily in caches, logs, or processing buffers, and may also retain access logs about who viewed which clip and when. If these data are kept longer than needed for playback delivery or security purposes, the storage limitation principle is violated.
assumptions: Assumes P2 maintains caches, logs, or temporary storage for retrieved clips or playback events.
